JUST IN: UP Diliman student Mattheo Wovi Villanueva has been released from Delpan Police Station 12 after posting bail amounting to P36,000, following four days in detention and hours of delay in processing his papers.

Villanueva was apprehended without a warrant at the Sept. 21 Mendiola rally while serving as a paralegal for a media officer. He was among the protesters beaten and arrested by police during the dispersal.

Four charges were lodged against Villanueva during his inquest last Wednesday night, including illegal assembly and resistance to authority, as well as unlawful assembly under Batas Pambansa 880, a Martial Law-era measure criticized by rights groups for curtailing freedom of assembly.

The cases have yet to be filed in court pending the resolution of the inquest.

data.raw_text:
*Baseless Allegations– A Global Phenomenon in ALL democracies, by ALL political dispensations – a general view*

Politics everywhere any time has always had its share of allegations, but in today’s world of 24/7 media and social platforms, baseless allegations spread faster and stick longer. From the US to Brazil, India to the UK, Kenya to France, Philippines to Japan and South Korea to Malaysia, baseless allegations have become political tools. They may fail in court or in fact-checks, but they succeed in their main goal: shaping perceptions, dividing societies, and undermining trust in institutions.

A major effect is delegitimising opponents, leaders or parties without evidence by tarnishing reputations. Even if proven false later, the damage to public trust is often permanent. Baseless allegations also shape narratives, in an era of *“perception politics”*, where allegations become tools to control headlines, distract from policy failures, or rally supporters. Emotional claims resonate more quickly with people than complex facts.
Among other dangerous outcomes is repeated baseless charges against courts, election bodies, or regulators weaken faith in institutions. Once trust is eroded, democratic systems suffer because people no longer believe in fair play. It normalises politics of suspicion rather than politics of ideas which is destabilising in the long run for any democracy. Citizens get trapped in a cycle of polarisation, *where truth matters less than loyalty*. Ultimately, governance suffers, because energy is spent on defending or attacking allegations rather than solving problems.

As a way forward citizens must cultivate critical thinking instead of accepting partisan claims at face value. Political culture should value evidence-based debate over mudslinging.

Of course, we are in a democracy where choices are available. The moot point is, should we be also contributing to this mayhem, either which way?

Stay well
